article.headline: The Algorithm Made Me Rich (Ask Me in a Year)
article.lede: A retail investor posting on X is celebrating a 25% year-to-date gain in a Roth IRA stocked entirely with semiconductor names selected by Claude, Anthropic's AI assistant. The basket — six companies spanning every link in the chip-packaging and electronics supply chain — has ridden the AI infrastructure wave almost perfectly. Whether the model deserves the credit is a different question entirely.
article.body:
The six names that @pepemoonboy assembled — Amkor Technology, Photronics, Celestica, ASE Technology, Fabrinet, and Onto Innovation — are not household names, but together they form something like a complete cross-section of the unglamorous infrastructure that makes AI hardware possible. Amkor (AMKR) and ASE Technology (ASX) are the two largest Western and Asian providers, respectively, of OSAT (Outsourced Assembly and Test) services: the factories that take finished silicon wafers from companies like TSMC and package them into the chips that end up in servers and smartphones. Advanced packaging — stacking dies in three dimensions, connecting them with microscopic copper pillars rather than traditional wire bonds — has become one of the most contested bottlenecks in AI manufacturing, and both companies are spending billions to expand capacity. ASE alone committed $7 billion in capital expenditure for 2026, with advanced packaging revenue expected to double to $3.2 billion over the year. Amkor, the leading Western OSAT provider with a sprawling new campus under construction in Peoria, Arizona, reported Q1 2026 revenue of $1.685 billion, up 27% year-over-year, and told investors its AI packaging portfolio would triple in the second half.

Photronics (PLAB) operates at an even earlier point in the manufacturing sequence, producing photomasks — the glass reticles onto which chip circuit patterns are etched using ultraviolet light, functioning as the stencils through which each generation of semiconductor is stamped into existence. It is a specialized, capital-intensive business with high barriers to entry, and Photronics holds a significant share of the global market from its eleven manufacturing facilities across Asia, Europe, and North America. The company reported Q1 2026 revenue of $225 million, up about 6% year-over-year, and maintains a balance sheet loaded with $588 million in cash against a $330 million capex plan — a financial profile that suggests patience rather than desperation. The photomask market expands each time chipmakers migrate to a smaller process node, which means Photronics benefits structurally from the same semiconductor density race that is driving AI compute demand.

Celestica (CLS) and Fabrinet (FN) occupy the EMS (Electronics Manufacturing Services) tier — the contract manufacturers who turn components into finished systems. Celestica has been one of the most dramatic beneficiaries of the AI infrastructure build-out, assembling the AI servers, networking switches, and storage hardware that hyperscalers order in enormous volumes. Its Q1 2026 revenue hit $4.05 billion, up 53% year-over-year, and the company raised its full-year 2026 target to $17 billion — a figure that would have seemed fantastical only two years ago. Fabrinet's specialization is narrower and more precise: the company manufactures the high-bandwidth optical transceivers that move data between chips and across data-center floors at the speed of light. As AI clusters scale, the demand for coherent optical interconnects — the fiber-based links that tie thousands of GPUs together — has grown faster than almost any segment in the supply chain. Fabrinet reported Q3 fiscal 2026 revenue of $1.21 billion, up 39% year-over-year, with optical communications alone accounting for 73% of that total. It carries zero debt.

Onto Innovation (ONTO) is the outlier in the basket, sitting upstream of all the others: it makes process-control metrology systems, the inspection and measurement equipment that semiconductor manufacturers use to verify that each fabrication step is executing within tolerance. As chip geometries have shrunk toward the angstrom scale and packaging architectures have grown in three-dimensional complexity, the need for precise measurement tools has become acute — a defect invisible at one process node can be catastrophic at the next. Onto recently invested $710 million for a 27% equity stake in Rigaku Holdings to expand its hybrid metrology capabilities, targeting a market expected to exceed $1 billion. The company's positioning is somewhat analogous to selling precision scales to a gold rush rather than panning for gold oneself.

The "AI-curated basket" phenomenon that the post illustrates — using Claude or ChatGPT to perform systematic fundamental analysis across a cohort of related stocks, then building a concentrated portfolio from the output — has become a recognizable subgenre of retail investing discourse in 2026. Surveys suggest roughly one in five retail investors already use AI tools for portfolio decisions, and the AI's output in this case is impressively thorough: the prompt visible in the screenshot requests eight quarters of revenue, margins, debt ratios, institutional ownership, insider activity, and earnings call transcripts. That is the research workflow of a small buy-side analyst, automated and compressed. What the AI cannot supply is what no financial analysis can supply in isolation: a sense of how much of the good news is already in the price, or whether the specific moment of entry happens to coincide with a macro tailwind that will eventually reverse.

The methodological caveat here is important and worth stating plainly. A 25% gain over four months in a basket of six AI-adjacent semiconductor names, entered at the beginning of a year when hyperscaler capital expenditure surged past $600 billion, tells us rather more about the cyclical momentum in AI infrastructure spending than about the model's stock-picking acumen. All six companies reported strong earnings; all six are direct beneficiaries of trends that were already well-documented when the positions were opened. Survivorship bias compounds the problem: the AI presumably analyzed these six companies because the human prompted it to — selecting a curated universe of AI-supply-chain names is itself an investment thesis, one that the poster, not the algorithm, implicitly endorsed. A single winning trade, even a striking one, is too small a sample to distinguish luck from skill, and the honest interpretation of a 25% YTD return is not that the machine is a good stock-picker but that the machine helped a human stay disciplined in a sector the human had already identified as promising. Whether the two are meaningfully different is the question that will take considerably longer than four months to answer.

concepts.definition: The segment of the semiconductor supply chain that handles the back-end steps of chip production: packaging finished silicon dies into protective housings, bonding wire connections, and testing completed chips before they ship to device manufacturers. Major OSATs include Amkor (Western) and ASE Technology (Taiwanese). Advanced packaging — techniques like 2.5D interposers and 3D die stacking — has made this once-commoditized business a critical bottleneck in AI chip supply.

A high-precision glass plate onto which the circuit pattern of a semiconductor layer is etched. During lithography, ultraviolet or extreme-ultraviolet light passes through the mask and projects the pattern onto a silicon wafer coated in photosensitive material. A single chip requires dozens of separate masks, one per process layer, and each mask must be accurate to within a fraction of a nanometer. Photronics is one of a handful of companies worldwide that manufactures them at scale.

Contract manufacturers who build finished electronic systems — servers, networking switches, storage arrays, optical modules — from components supplied by their customers. EMS providers like Celestica and Fabrinet do not design the products; they supply the manufacturing infrastructure, engineering expertise, and supply-chain management that allow technology companies to scale production without building their own factories. The AI infrastructure boom has made EMS providers an indirect but large beneficiary of hyperscaler capital expenditure.

The science of measuring semiconductor structures during and after fabrication to verify that each step — deposition, etching, lithography, chemical-mechanical planarization — has executed within the required dimensional tolerances. At modern chip nodes, features measure only a few nanometers across; a deviation of a single angstrom can shift yield from acceptable to catastrophic. Metrology systems from companies like Onto Innovation are used by chipmakers to catch process drift before it propagates through an entire wafer lot.

A family of semiconductor assembly techniques that go beyond traditional wire-bond packaging by integrating multiple dies — logic chips, memory, and I/O — into a single compact module. Methods include 2.5D integration (chips side-by-side on a silicon interposer) and 3D stacking (chips bonded face-to-face with through-silicon vias). Advanced packaging dramatically reduces the distance electrical signals must travel, improving performance and energy efficiency, and has become essential for AI accelerators that pair large GPU dies with high-bandwidth memory.

article.fact_check: Financial figures sourced from company earnings releases and financial newswires: Amkor Q1 2026 revenue $1.685B (+27% YoY), ASE 2026 capex $7B and advanced packaging revenue doubling to $3.2B, Celestica Q1 2026 revenue $4.05B (+53% YoY) and full-year target $17B, Fabrinet Q3 FY2026 revenue $1.21B (+39% YoY), Photronics Q1 FY2026 revenue $225M (+6% YoY), Onto Innovation Rigaku stake $710M for 27% equity. Hyperscaler capex figure ($600B+ in 2026) is sourced from industry estimates. YTD portfolio performance figures ($78,943.35 balance, +$15,877.36, +25.18%) are taken directly from the screenshots in the original post. The claim that roughly 1 in 5 retail investors use AI tools for portfolio decisions is consistent with survey data cited in financial media.

ticker_asx.name: ASE Technology Holding Co., Ltd.
ticker_asx.blurb: ASE Technology is the world's largest OSAT (outsourced semiconductor assembly and test) company, responsible for packaging and testing chips after they leave the foundry wafer fab. Chip packaging — the process of cutting wafers into individual dies, mounting them in substrates, and connecting them to the outside world — is increasingly strategic as advanced packaging (chiplets, CoWoS, SoIC) becomes essential for AI accelerators that exceed the reticle size limits of individual dies. ASE's CoWoS-compatible packaging capacity has become a key bottleneck in NVIDIA Blackwell GPU supply chains. ASE is headquartered in Kaohsiung, Taiwan.
ticker_asx.recent: ASE has benefited from surging demand for advanced packaging from AI chip supply chains. NVIDIA's Blackwell GPUs require CoWoS advanced packaging, a significant portion of which flows through ASE and its competitor SPIL (a subsidiary). Forward P/E of ~47.4x on 39.7% projected EPS growth yields a PEG of 1.19. Revenue growth is driven by advanced packaging volumes rather than legacy wire-bond assembly.

ticker_fn.description: Fabrinet is a precision contract manufacturer specializing in optical and electro-optical components and assemblies, primarily the high-bandwidth transceivers and interconnects used in AI data center networking. Operating primarily from Thailand, it serves the world's leading optical networking and photonics companies. As AI clusters have scaled, demand for 400G/800G/1.6T coherent optical transceivers — the physical links that move data between GPU clusters — has made Fabrinet one of the fastest-growing EMS companies in the sector. Q3 FY2026 revenue was $1.21 billion (+39% YoY); the company carries zero debt and $945 million in cash.

ticker_onto.description: Onto Innovation is a semiconductor process-control equipment company providing inspection, metrology (precision measurement), lithography, and software solutions used to verify and control chip fabrication at the nanometer scale. Its systems are used at leading-edge fabs to measure structural dimensions in gate-all-around transistors, high-bandwidth memory cells, and advanced packaging interconnects. In 2025-2026, Onto invested $710 million for a 27% equity stake in Rigaku Holdings to expand into hybrid X-ray metrology, targeting a $1 billion+ addressable market. The company's flagship Atlas G6 OCD metrology platform targets second-generation GAA logic and DRAM nodes for AI chips.
